title: Tiered Clarity Lanes — UX & economics scratch
content:
High-level idea: provide lightweight end-user controls + implicit routing that let applications pick a tradeoff between answer clarity/detail and cost/latency. Call this concept 'Clarity Lanes' — discrete output modes (e.g. Brief, Normal, Deep) with predictable unit economics and UX affordances.

Why: lots of product teams ask for ways to reduce token cost while keeping user experience acceptable. Current approach (manual prompt edits, model switching, ad-hoc heuristics) is noisy for product teams and inconsistent for end users. Clarity Lanes give a single mental model for product devs and users: choose the lane, get consistent behavior and measurable cost.

Goals (MVP):
- Expose 3 lanes: brief, normal, deep. Each lane maps to a runtime config: model variant (or size), max tokens, temperature/brevity heuristics, and optional semantic compression/summary step.
- Provide SDK + REST flags (clarity_lane: "brief" | "normal" | "deep") and a fallback routing policy in the platform if the requested lane cannot be served at desired latency/cost.
- Surface estimated token cost and expected latency in-console and in SDK helper methods.
- Capture telemetry for per-lane quality metrics (human rating, perplexity proxies, hallucination signals) and per-lane unit economics (tokens, GPU ms).

Non-goals (MVP):
- User-facing editor for crafting lane semantics (that's a follow-up).
- Fine-grained per-request quality tuning beyond the three lanes.

User stories (product-facing):
1) As a mobile product PM, I want to let users pick "Brief" mode so we can reduce monthly token spend for heavy users and test retention impact. Acceptance: flag toggles in SDK, console shows expected monthly cost delta when switching baseline to "Brief" for sample traffic.
2) As a platform operator, I want lanes to be routable to different capacity pools (cheap batched GPU for brief, low-latency pool for deep) so we can maintain latency SLOs and unit economics. Acceptance: routing policy objects exist and can be attached to lane config.
3) As a developer, I want an API to ask for cost/latency estimates for a lane given sample input (prompt length) so I can decide defaults in my app. Acceptance: /estimate endpoint returning tokens and ms distribution.

Runtime mapping (brainstorm):
- Brief: smaller model / aggressive max_tokens limit / decoding heuristics + light prefix compression. Target: <= 50 tokens, 0.6 temperature, use 4-bit quantized variant where possible.
- Normal: baseline model + sensible max_tokens (150-300) and balanced temperature.
- Deep: larger model or larger sequence limit, allow chain-of-thought style outputs with longer max_tokens and slightly higher temperature for exploratory answers.

UX patterns:
- End-user toggle on the assistant UI: Brief / Normal / Deep with microcopy describing tradeoffs and a small cost badge ("~25% cheaper").
- API flag for programmatic control and per-request override.
- Console viz: per-lane consumption heatmap, per-lane average latency, and per-lane quality score (human-review sample rate).
- Fallback UI guidance: if Deep is unavailable due to capacity, return Normal + hint metadata to client for graceful degrade.

Metrics to track (initial):
- Per-lane avg tokens per request
- Per-lane avg latency P50/P95
- Per-lane cost per 1k requests
- Downstream retention/engagement delta for users exposed to Brief vs Normal (product experiment)
- Quality regression signals (differences in model scoring on seeded eval prompts)

Experiment plan (A/B):
- A/B test 1: default lane for new users = Normal (control) vs Brief (treatment). Track short-term engagement (7-day DAU) and token consumption. Run for 14 days or until N=10k users.
- A/B test 2: show cost badge vs no cost badge when switching lanes, measure conversion to cheaper lane and satisfaction surveys.

Operational considerations / risks:
- Risk: users gaming the system by setting Brief globally and expecting high-quality output for complex queries. Mitigation: provide prompt-level overrides and educate product teams via docs.
- Risk: lane semantics drift as models and quantization profiles change. Mitigation: tie lane config to model-version pinning and maintain per-lane regression tests / eval suites.
- Risk: increased complexity for routing and capacity planning. Mitigation: lane can be a soft hint initially; platform may map lanes to capacity pools but allow polyfill fallbacks.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How many lanes are optimal? Starting with 3 seems simple; do we need an "ultra-brief" later for edge devices?
- Do we expose a cost budget instead of lanes (e.g., token budget per session)? Pros/cons.
- Exact runtime mappings (model names / quantization) — need SRE + runtime alignment.
- What guardrails for hallucination exposure per lane? E.g., disable chain-of-thought for Brief.

Immediate next actions (this week):
- Sync 30m with runtime + serving runtime (Rohan + Mira + Kiera) to sketch model-variant mappings and rough latency targets. (Blockers: confirm available quantized builds, reserved pool options).
- Draft console mock for per-lane usage and cost badge (Devon to produce quick Figma frames).
- Create ticket PROD-3421 to track implementation backlog and link simple /estimate API prototype.

Longer-term ideas (parking lot):
- Per-intent lanes: different clarity for different intent classes (code, email, QA).
- Adaptive lanes: system toggles lane automatically based on current user quota or latency pressure with explicit UX signal.
- Lane-presets for enterprise customers with custom SLAs and price schedules.

Notes to self: keep the lane names consumer-friendly but unambiguous. Avoid engineering jargon in the UIs ("Normal" not "Standard-v2").

Write-up length: this is a brain-dump — next version should be a tightened PRD with explicit API spec, test cases, and rollout timeline.

End of notes.
